title: Return to SEND(er)
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a school inclusion leader in Victoria, Australia, reacts to the state's announced changes to the Disability Inclusion Profile. The tool will assess 26 activities instead of 31, student-level funding rates will fall 2.5 percent, and mainstream schools will lose $850 per term per eligible student from 2027. Brien argues that the old system already rewarded schools skilled at producing documentation more than those building inclusive practice. He shows that seven activities on which his school often scored 'substantial' are now condensed into four, so students who barely qualified will lose funding. He warns that schools with strong tier 1 instruction, a low floor and high ceiling, will be funded least, and that the changes will add to administrative load rather than reduce it.
points: The revised profile condenses overlapping activities while leaving the funding threshold unchanged, so fewer students will qualify.
The stated aim of reducing administrative workload is doubtful because schools must now find new evidence across other activities.
Schools that are truly inclusive through strong tier 1 teaching are likely to receive the least funding.
A 2.5 percent rate cut and a $850 per term reduction for mainstream schools land in the same week full funding for Victorian schools was announced for 2034.
Brien describes an uncomfortable tension in which his role exists to check funding boxes while also improving inclusive practice.
quotes: I believed this created a system that was less about creating inclusive teaching practices for our students with most needs and more schools that were skilled in creating the documentation they needed to attain funding.
There’s an irony in the above statement where the current 31 different measured activities have been condensed into 26.
In simple terms, this new set of activities is likely to mean that many students who just scraped through for funding currently, are not going to be funded for the support they still need in future.
It’s a little hard to see (without yet seeing the further information to be released) how this actually reduces the administrative workload of schools and seemingly is going to add to it
I often criticise the way that schools utilise their funding, but the funding for students with additional needs really seems like a non-negotiable need.
we are further punishing schools that are being truly inclusive by creating a low floor and high ceiling in their tier 1 instruction and curriculum resources to meet the needs of all learners.
The most inclusive environments are likely to be the least funded.
Less and harder to gain funding just means that our most vulnerable learners are going to be further negatively impacted by the education system and their opportunities in life diminished.
